name: Japanese Imperial Ultranationalism
description: The late imperial Japanese doctrine of kokutai: emperor-centred national unity, imperial mission and mobilisation. It is distinct from German Nazism and from every earlier or later form of Japanese nationalism.
period: Official kokutai and imperial mobilisation doctrine, 1937–1945
scope: The official late-imperial political doctrine articulated in Kokutai no hongi and national mobilisation, checked against contemporary documents. It excludes a blanket identification with Nazism and does not equate all Japanese people, all Shinto believers or every ultranationalist faction with this doctrine.
phrase: A society united in service to the emperor and national polity, coordinating education, economic life and public duties to sustain Japan’s imperial mission.

sources.title: The US-Japan War Talks: background and official documents
sources.publisher: Japan Center for Asian Historical Records

axes: The imperial polity rejects individualist parliamentary supremacy and places loyal institutions beneath emperor-centred national unity. Parties give way to a national mobilisation association.
Military influence and civilian officials coexist; the emperor’s authority does not imply that every autonomous military coup is doctrinally legitimate.

Kokutai presents national life as an emperor-centred family order, with imported ideas to be transformed through the Japanese polity. Imperial cultural hierarchy differs from plural national equality.
Adoption of useful foreign knowledge is not equivalent to recognition of parallel public cultures. Claimed Asian solidarity coexists with coercive imperial assimilation.

Diplomacy and military command remain instrumental; opposition to autonomous coups is distinct from opposition to external war.

Economic activity is subordinated to collective national service, but mobilisation preserves substantial private ownership. Control of firms cannot be treated as nationalisation.
Private industrial groups coexist with public strategic activity. Anti-individualism is not itself public ownership; each ownership mechanism is assessed separately.

Mobilisation does not prohibit all trade or imported technology; useful foreign transactions qualify autarkic tendencies.

Imperial sacred ancestry and prescribed national ritual underpin government legitimacy and moral formation. State Shinto was officially described as civic rather than a private religion, but this does not make sacred public authority secular.
Compulsory civic observance applied across private religious identities. Buddhist and other traditions existed; clerical legislative control is distinct from emperor-centred sacral state authority.

Technical modernisation is not progressive family policy. State moral education can limit parental authority even within traditional family norms.

Useful Western knowledge is to be absorbed and transformed through the national polity. Mobilisation favours productive capability, while bodily experimentation can conflict with family continuity and disciplined collective safeguards.
National technological strength does not automatically establish support for every risky medical technique. Modern climate and AI items are expressly hypothetical translations.

Neighbourhood organisation is local implementation rather than constitutionally protected local autonomy. Imperial territorial hierarchy is not an equal federal compact.

National ancestry is central to legitimacy, while schooling and moral discipline actively cultivate loyalty and behaviour. Sacred lineage must not be converted into claims about every psychological trait or Nazi racial genetics.
This source establishes moral-cultural formation and lineage symbolism, not modern genetic science. Some sex/temperament claims are mixed; the racial violence and pay-gap premises remain problematic.
